headline: Burned Scrolls Reveal Ancient Secrets With X-Ray Breakthrough
meta_description: Scientists discovered that lead in ancient ink makes carbonized scrolls readable via X-ray scans, potentially unlocking 2,000-year-old texts from Mount Vesuviu…
summary_short: Researchers burned their own papyrus scrolls to prove that tiny amounts of lead in ancient ink can unlock hidden texts from Herculaneum's charred library.
body:
For nearly 2,000 years, over a thousand papyrus scrolls buried by Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. have sat largely unread in collections across Italy, France, and England—too fragile to safely unroll without crumbling to ash. Now, UC Berkeley scientist Douglas Seiler and his team have discovered a way to read them without touching them at all. By intentionally burning papyrus scrolls inscribed with passages from the Bible, Star Wars, and classic television, they found that tiny amounts of lead in ancient ink absorb X-rays up to 25 times more powerfully than carbonized paper. This stark contrast allows computers to virtually flatten the rolled sheets and expose hidden writing—potentially unlocking lost works of Greek and Roman philosophy, literature, and science that vanished from history.

Seiler's experimental approach was painstaking: he obtained authentic papyrus and reed pens from Egypt, traditional Japanese lampblack ink, and even recruited high school students to write on the scrolls before carbonizing them in a furnace. The results, published in September 2026 in PLOS ONE, show that even a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner can detect lead-based ink in burned scrolls, offering a straightforward screening tool. This matters profoundly because earlier attempts to physically open the scrolls—beginning after their discovery in 1752—were often catastrophic, reducing irreplaceable texts to piles of dust. Among the few successfully opened scrolls were works by Philodemus, an Epicurean philosopher who lived in Herculaneum before the eruption.

Leah Packard-Grams, a Berkeley papyrologist who consulted on the project, calls the potential stakes "practically unquantifiable." Unlike most ancient texts that survive only as copies made by later scribes, these Herculaneum scrolls are originals—direct windows into Roman intellectual life, frozen in time by catastrophe. The library represents one of antiquity's rarest treasures: voices that might otherwise have been lost forever.
quick_facts: Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E., burying over 1,000 scrolls in Herculaneum
Lead in ancient ink absorbs up to 25 times more X-rays than burned papyrus
About 1,800 scrolls and fragments survive in collections across Italy, France, and England
Early attempts to physically unroll scrolls often reduced them to ash
